title: "How to Fix Neovim's gq / gw Randomly Indenting Paragraphs"
author: "Andre Mirończuk"
date: "2026-08-17"
categories: [Neovim]
image: "./gq_gw_thumbnail.png"
execute:
  freeze: true
---

TLDR:  
Neovim thinks you are writing C with the default settings when smartindent is set to
true. Clear the cinwords opt (`vim.opt.cinwords = {}` or `:set cinwords=`).

Have you ever formatted your prose in a markdown/txt file with the built-in formatter
and got weird extra indentation?

Example:
```markdown
I tried writing a deeply moving novel about my existential dread, but my editor had
for some bizarre reason decided that my emotional narrative was actually C code, so
        now my deepest confession is sitting here indented like a nested loop.
```

This happens when smartindent is set to true (non-default) and cinwords set is
populated (by default it's `cinwords=if,else,while,do,for,switch`). When it just so
happens that after formatting a line according to the `textwidth` the new line starts
with one of those words, the following line is indented based on `shiftwidth` (the
default is 8).

To reproduce (v0.12.6):

1. Open clean Neovim
```bash
nvim --clean
```

2. Set these settings
```
:set smartindent
```
```
:set textwidth=85
```

3. Paste this text

```markdown
I tried writing a deeply moving novel about my existential dread, but my editor had for some bizarre reason decided that my emotional narrative was actually C code, so now my deepest confession is sitting here indented like a nested loop.
```

4. Put your cursor on this line and press `gqq` or `gww` or `gqip` or `gwip`

Result:

```markdown
I tried writing a deeply moving novel about my existential dread, but my editor had
for some bizarre reason decided that my emotional narrative was actually C code, so
        now my deepest confession is sitting here indented like a nested loop.
```

Tips:  
If you are using `gq`, consider switching to `gw`. `gw` automatically preserves the
cursor position and it does not use formatprg and formatexpr, that can be set
depending on what plugins do you use (for example `conform.nvim`).

Keymaps you might like:
```lua
vim.keymap.set('n', '<A-q>', 'gwip', { noremap = true })

-- Like Ctrl+v, but it will immediately format the line according to the textwidth, if set
vim.keymap.set('i', '<M-C-V>', '<C-R>+', { noremap = true })
vim.keymap.set('n', '<M-C-V>', function()
  vim.cmd('normal! "+p')
  vim.cmd('normal! gww')
end, { noremap = true })
```
